title: EC-Council CND
summary: The Certified Network Defender (CND) from EC-Council is a defensive certification for network and security operations staff who protect an enterprise network rather than attack it. It sits at a mid level, above first line support and below advanced incident response or forensics credentials, and it suits network administrators moving into security operations, junior analysts and system administrators with security duties. It proves to an employer that you can read network traffic, harden devices, apply the right controls and follow an incident through to containment and recovery. The exam is multiple choice and scenario driven, so it tests decisions about traffic and configuration rather than the terms alone. The published domains and weightings are set out below. It leads to roles such as network security engineer, security operations analyst, network defender and infrastructure security administrator. This is an independent study guide and is not official EC-Council material; confirm the current blueprint with the vendor before you book.

beginner.definition: The Certified Network Defender is a security certificate from EC-Council. It is about defending a network instead of breaking into one. Network means the cables, switches, routers and wireless links that carry data between computers. You learn how to protect that path from attackers.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most attacks reach a victim over a network. Employers need people who can watch and protect that path. This certificate shows that you understand both the attack and the defence. It is a natural next step for a network administrator who wants to move into security. It also prepares you for the more advanced defensive and investigative certifications.
howItWorks: Learn the fundamentals first, such as how data moves through the layers of a network.
Study the common network attacks, including denial of service, address spoofing and attacks on wireless links.
Practise with the defensive devices you will meet at work. These include firewalls and intrusion detection systems.
Learn how to write a security policy and how to harden a device against attack.
Train on monitoring and incident response, because a defender must notice and contain an attack quickly.
The exam is multiple choice with scenario questions. Practise choosing the best response to a described event.
beginner.example: Imagine a staff laptop that suddenly sends large amounts of data to an unknown address overseas. A network defender does not simply unplug the laptop and move on. You check the firewall and intrusion detection logs. You look at the domain name server queries and confirm whether the traffic is encrypted. Then you work out whether other machines talk to the same address. Then you isolate the host and start the response process. This exam tests that whole chain of thought.
takeaways: Know your network first. You cannot defend traffic flows you do not understand.
Learn the defensive controls and the attacks together, because exam scenarios mix them.
The weight sits on controls, policies and monitoring. Do not spend all your time on attack theory.

objectives: Explain how data moves through a network and where it can be attacked
Identify common network attacks and the weaknesses they exploit
Configure firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention systems, and virtual private networks
Write and apply network security policy, hardening baselines and access control
Monitor network traffic and detect suspicious activity
Respond to a network incident, contain it and support recovery

chapters.title: Network security fundamentals
objectives: Explain defence in depth and how each layer of protection supports the others
Describe how data moves through the layers of a network model and where faults occur
Identify network devices and topologies and explain the security risk each one adds
Apply the ideas of least privilege and network segmentation to a simple design
Relate network security policy to the compliance duties an organisation must meet

chapters.title: Network security threats and vulnerabilities
objectives: Recognise common network attacks and describe how each one works
Identify vulnerabilities in network infrastructure and explain how attackers use them
Analyse wireless threats such as rogue access points and interception of traffic
Spot social engineering and insider threat indicators in a scenario
Explain why a zero day vulnerability is hard to defend and what reduces the exposure

chapters.title: Network security controls, protocols and devices
objectives: Configure firewall rules and access control lists that allow only the traffic you intend
Deploy intrusion detection and prevention systems and tune them to reduce false alarms
Choose and configure virtual private network and encryption protocols for remote access
Configure web application firewalls, proxy servers and network access control
Apply authentication standards for wired and wireless network access

chapters.title: Network security policy design and implementation
objectives: Design security policies and procedures that staff can actually follow
Apply hardening baselines and secure configuration to network devices
Implement access control models and identity management for network users
Run patch and configuration management so known weaknesses are closed
Audit configuration against policy and record the exceptions you accept

chapters.title: Network security monitoring and incident response
objectives: Collect and correlate network logs in a monitoring platform so events can be investigated
Analyse network traffic and detect behaviour that does not match the normal pattern
Follow an incident response process from detection through containment and recovery
Run vulnerability assessments and interpret the results in priority order
Use threat intelligence and network evidence to support an investigation
